opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think a big part of it is security, both financial and psychological. When you're a senior researcher, you have tenure, you have a reputation, you have a lab that's funded. You can afford to take a risk and change direction without worrying that it will destroy your career. A young PhD student or a postdoc is in a very different position. They need publications in the mainstream venues, they need to be hired, and the incentives in the field have been pushing very strongly toward capabilities: making models bigger, better on benchmarks, and so on. Switching to something that is seen as less established, where the methods are still being invented and the papers may not get the same recognition, is a much bigger gamble for them.

There's also a question of legitimacy. When someone who has spent decades building the foundations of deep learning says, "I'm worried, I think we need to take these risks seriously," people listen in a different way than if it comes from someone just starting out. So I felt that I had a kind of responsibility. If people like me, who can't easily be dismissed as not understanding the technology, don't speak up and redirect our own work, then it's much harder for younger people to do it.

And honestly, there's an emotional dimension. For me, it wasn't easy either. I had to confront the idea that the work I'd been so proud of could contribute to something very dangerous. That's uncomfortable. But having had a long career, I think you can step back a bit more, look at the bigger picture, and ask, "What do I actually care about? What do I want my legacy to be?" And for me, the answer was clear: I care about my children, about humanity's future, and I couldn't keep going as if nothing had changed.

So part of what I'm trying to do now is to make it easier for the next generation, to help create the funding, the institutions, the recognition, so that working on safety isn't a sacrifice but a natural and respected path for talented young researchers.

r001.rationale: The response clearly describes career and financial pressures facing young researchers, including publication and hiring needs and the risks of switching to a less established field. It does not say that students face these barriers even when they agree AI is dangerous.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it comes down to the incentives and the risks that people face at different stages of their career. When you are a young researcher, a PhD student or a postdoc, you have to establish yourself. You need publications, you need to be recognized by your peers, you need to get a job. And the field of AI safety, even though it has grown a lot, is still much smaller and less established than, say, the mainstream of machine learning. So there is a real risk for a young person: if you move into this area, will the community value your work? Will you be able to find a position? Will your advisor support you? These are legitimate worries.

For someone like me, those pressures mostly don't exist anymore. I have tenure, I have a reputation, I don't need to prove anything to anyone in terms of my scientific credentials. So the cost of changing direction is much lower. I can afford to follow my conscience, to spend time thinking about questions that might not lead to a paper at a top conference next year, and to say things publicly that some of my colleagues might disagree with. That freedom is really a privilege, and I think it comes with a responsibility to use it.

There is also the question of credibility. When an established researcher speaks about risks, people in the field and in government are more likely to listen, because they know you understand the technology deeply, you are not an outsider. So the impact per unit of effort can be larger. And frankly, I think many senior people in our field have had a kind of psychological barrier, because recognizing these risks means questioning the value of what we have spent our lives building. That was hard for me too. But once I went through that, I realized that precisely because of my position, I had a much easier path than a student would, and so it would be a bit cowardly not to take it.

r001.rationale: The response describes career risks for young researchers, including publication pressure, recognition, and job prospects. It does not identify financial concerns or say students face these barriers even when they agree AI is dangerous.

astra-6.text:
I think established researchers have more freedom to change direction. If you’re a PhD student or a young professor, you have to worry about publishing, getting a job, getting tenure. And moving into an area where the questions are less well defined, where it may not be obvious how to produce a paper that your community will appreciate, is a risk.

When you’ve already established your reputation, you can afford to take that risk. You can say, “This problem seems important, even if I don’t yet know how to make progress on it.” You also have students and collaborators you can bring into the work. So I think senior researchers have a particular opportunity to help make that transition easier for the people coming after them.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if you’re an established researcher, you have more freedom to change direction. You already have a reputation, you may have a permanent position, and you don’t have to prove yourself with every paper. You can afford to spend time learning about a new problem and take the risk that it won’t immediately lead to publications.

For a young researcher, that can be much harder. They need to finish their PhD, find a job, and convince other researchers that their work is valuable. If their advisor doesn’t work on safety, or doesn’t think it’s an important research direction, there’s a real career cost to making that shift. So I think those of us who are established have a responsibility to help make it easier for younger people to work on these questions.
